CISA: Critical VMware RCE flaw now exploited by ransomware gangs
bleepingcomputer.com · 15 Sep 2026 12:16 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.6-terra
TAGSbroadcomcisacve-2024-37079cve-2025-22225cve-2026-22719cve-2026-59310directory-traversalquirsoransomware-gangsreverse-sshshadowserverunited-statesvmwarevmware-esxivmware-vcenter-server
98
In plain words

The U.S. cyber agency CISA says ransomware groups are now using a serious weakness in VMware vCenter, software many organizations use to manage virtual computers and the data on them. Broadcom released a fix in July, but attackers had already compromised systems in 47 countries and used the weakness to keep remote access. This matters because taking control of these systems can give criminals a route into an organization’s network and sensitive information, and they may then lock systems or data to demand payment.

Summary
CISA warns that ransomware groups are actively exploiting the critical VMware vCenter directory traversal RCE flaw CVE-2026-59310, which was patched in July. Organizations should urgently patch exposed vCenter servers, as attackers have already used the flaw for reverse SSH persistence.

CISA has updated its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog to warn that ransomware gangs are actively abusing CVE-2026-59310, a critical VMware vCenter flaw. Broadcom patched the issue on July 29 and described it as a directory traversal weakness in the vCenter Syslog server. Unauthenticated attackers can exploit it to execute arbitrary code, and Broadcom advised customers to treat patching as an emergency.

Within two weeks of the patch, DFIR firm QUIRSO reported that a suspected advanced persistent threat actor had exploited the flaw to compromise more than 361 IP addresses across 47 countries. The actor deployed a reverse SSH tool to maintain access and remotely control affected systems. CISA added the flaw to its catalog in August and directed U.S. government agencies to secure affected vCenter systems within three days.

VMware servers are frequent ransomware targets because compromised vCenter or ESXi systems can provide access to an organization’s network and internally stored sensitive data. Shadowserver tracks more than 450 VMware vCenter servers exposed online, though it is unknown how many have been patched. Over the past five years, CISA has marked 26 VMware vulnerabilities as exploited in the wild, including nine that were also used by ransomware operations.

  • The threat escalated quickly: Broadcom issued the patch on July 29, suspected attackers were reported exploiting the flaw within two weeks, and CISA subsequently identified ransomware use.
  • The reported compromise activity was geographically broad, with more than 361 IP addresses affected across 47 countries.
  • Internet exposure remains a concern because Shadowserver tracks more than 450 VMware vCenter servers online, while the number patched against this flaw is unknown.
  • VMware is a recurring ransomware target: CISA has listed 26 VMware vulnerabilities as exploited in the wild over the past five years, including nine linked to ransomware operations.
Key Points
  • 01CISA updated its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog to state that ransomware gangs are actively exploiting the critical VMware vCenter flaw CVE-2026-59310.
  • 02Broadcom patched CVE-2026-59310 on July 29 and described it as a critical directory traversal issue in the vCenter Syslog server that unauthenticated attackers can use to execute arbitrary code.
  • 03QUIRSO reported that a suspected advanced persistent threat actor compromised more than 361 IP addresses across 47 countries by exploiting the flaw and deploying a reverse SSH tool for persistence and remote access.
  • 04CISA added CVE-2026-59310 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog in August and ordered U.S. government agencies to secure affected vCenter systems within three days.
  • 05Shadowserver tracks more than 450 VMware vCenter servers exposed online, although it is not known how many have been patched against CVE-2026-59310.

    In plain words

    The article warns that a serious flaw in Cisco Secure Email Gateway devices lets an attacker take full control of a device simply by sending it a specially made email. Organizations using affected Cisco email gateway software—including physical devices and virtual versions—are at risk, and Cisco says the flaw has already been used in real attacks. Because these devices receive email from the internet and can handle an organization’s incoming mail, a takeover could let attackers read messages, steal information, remain inside the network, and move to other systems. Cisco has released updates, and updating is the only way to fix the problem.

    Summary
    Cisco Secure Email Gateway appliances running vulnerable AsyncOS releases can be remotely compromised as root by sending a crafted email, with exploitation reportedly active in the wild. Organizations should immediately upgrade to Cisco’s fixed builds and investigate any previously exposed appliances for compromise.

    CVE-2026-76461 is a critical SQL injection vulnerability in the email parsing logic of Cisco AsyncOS Software for Cisco Secure Email Gateway. An attacker can send a crafted email containing SQL statements that are executed while the appliance processes the message, without credentials, user interaction, or management-interface access. Successful exploitation can result in arbitrary operating-system command execution with root privileges.

    The vulnerability affects physical and virtual Cisco Secure Email Gateway deployments running releases 15.5 and earlier, 16.0, and 16.5. Cisco reported awareness of exploitation in the wild in September 2026, and CISA added the issue to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. Cisco released fixed AsyncOS builds, states there are no configuration workarounds, and recommends organizations patch promptly, review mail logs for COPY statements paired with TO PROGRAM, and treat exposed unpatched appliances as potentially compromised.

    • The initial attack path uses normal inbound email traffic, so limiting management-interface access or segmenting interfaces does not prevent exploitation of this flaw.
    • Because successful exploitation gives root-level control, an appliance that was reachable while unpatched should be treated as potentially compromised even after it is updated.
    • Exposure estimates based on service fingerprints identify systems that may be running affected software, not confirmed vulnerable versions, so organizations need to verify their exact AsyncOS build numbers.
    • Clustered email gateway deployments require investigation and patching of every member, since each appliance may be individually reachable and a partial update can leave exposure behind.
    Key Points
    • 01CVE-2026-76461 is a critical SQL injection flaw in Cisco AsyncOS email parsing that allows an attacker to send a crafted email and execute commands with root privileges without authentication or user interaction.
    • 02The issue affects Cisco Secure Email Gateway appliances and virtual deployments running AsyncOS 15.5 and earlier, 16.0, or 16.5, while Cisco Secure Email and Web Manager and Cisco Secure Web Appliance are reported as unaffected.
    • 03Cisco reported awareness of exploitation in the wild in September 2026, and CISA added the vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.
    • 04Cisco released fixed AsyncOS builds for affected release trains, and the article states that patching is the only remediation because no configuration workaround exists.
    • 05Organizations should review IronPort text mail logs for COPY statements paired with TO PROGRAM, check every member of clustered deployments, and monitor unexpected outbound connections from mail appliances.

China-Linked Hackers Exploit Chrome-Windows Zero-Day Chain to Deploy GRIMWEDGE
thehackernews.com · 15 Sep 2026 05:31 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.6-terra
TAGSbrowser-sandbox-escapechinacve-2026-85046dll-sideloadinggooglegrimwedgejunglebamboolongtalemicrosoftprocess-injectionreflected-xssspearphishingsuperstompunited-statesuta0560
96
In plain words

China-linked hacking groups sent targeted emails to nonprofit organizations, using links that secretly took victims to harmful websites and took advantage of weaknesses in Chrome and Windows. Once someone clicked, the attackers could install programs that survey the computer, read files, run commands, and in one case steal browser logins, cookies, and other private activity. The incident matters because fixes had appeared in Chrome’s public code but were not yet available in the regular Chrome version people use, leaving a window for attackers to act before updates reached users.

Summary
China-linked groups UTA0560 and JungleBamboo exploited a Chrome and Windows patch gap through spear-phishing links to deploy GRIMWEDGE and LONGTALE malware against NGOs. The campaign shows how publicly visible Chromium fixes can remain exploitable as zero-days in Chrome until stable releases ship.

Volexity attributed a September 1, 2026 spear-phishing campaign against multiple NGOs to the China-linked threat cluster UTA0560. The emails directed recipients through a reflected cross-site scripting flaw on a U.S.-based university website to attacker-controlled infrastructure. That infrastructure delivered a multi-stage Chrome and Windows exploit chain called BlueMoon to systems using Chrome on Windows.

The chain used CVE-2026-85046 to gain read/write access in Chrome’s V8 sandbox, CVE-2026-87491 to escape the browser sandbox, and CVE-2026-85880 to inject code into Chrome and execute code. UTA0560 used the chain to deploy GRIMWEDGE, a JavaScript backdoor that can profile systems, manage files and processes, run commands, and download additional payloads. Volexity also saw JungleBamboo use the same chain to install LONGTALE, a credential-stealing Chrome extension, while noting that the Chrome bugs had been fixed in Chromium source code but had not yet reached stable Chrome releases, creating a patch-gap exploitation window.

  • The attackers used a legitimate U.S.-based university website with a reflected XSS flaw as an initial redirect, which made the phishing links appear to point to a trusted destination before sending recipients to attacker-controlled infrastructure.
  • The exploit server filtered visitors to target only systems running Chrome on Windows, limiting exposure of the exploit chain and helping avoid analysis by irrelevant visitors.
  • Although the Chrome flaws had been fixed in Chromium’s open-source code, they were not yet included in a stable Chrome release, creating a patch-gap window in which they remained zero-days against Chrome users.
  • GRIMWEDGE has no built-in persistence, lateral movement, or dedicated data-exfiltration feature, but its file-reading, command-running, and payload-upload functions still provide sufficient access for UTA0560 to survey hosts and deploy further tools.
  • JungleBamboo’s LONGTALE extension focused on credential theft and surveillance rather than remote code execution, collecting browser data and sending it to its command server about every 30 seconds.
Key Points
  • 01Volexity attributed a September 1, 2026 spear-phishing campaign targeting multiple NGOs to the China-linked threat cluster UTA0560.
  • 02The campaign used a reflected cross-site scripting flaw on a U.S.-based university website to redirect victims to a Chrome and Windows exploit chain.
  • 03The chain combined CVE-2026-85046 and CVE-2026-87491 in Chrome with CVE-2026-85880 in Windows to obtain code execution in the Chrome browser process.
  • 04UTA0560 used the chain to install GRIMWEDGE, a JavaScript backdoor that can collect system information, manage files and processes, execute commands, and download additional payloads.
  • 05Volexity also observed JungleBamboo using the same chain to deploy LONGTALE, a fake Google Gemini Chrome extension that steals cookies, session data, keystrokes, and browser activity.

Human Attacker Exploits Marimo RCE, Reaches SSH Bastion in Eight Seconds
thehackernews.com · 15 Sep 2026 11:52 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.6-terra
TAGSamazon-web-services-secrets-manageraof-authorized-keys-injectionasyncsshcve-2021-33044cve-2021-33045cve-2026-39987dahua-ip-cameraslua-sandbox-escapemarimomongodbredisredis-rogue-replicationsysdigwordpressxmrig

In plain words

A skilled attacker used a serious flaw in Marimo, a notebook application, to take control of a system and reach another protected computer in only eight seconds. They used cloud access details found on the first system to retrieve a private login key and enter an SSH bastion, a gateway computer used to access other systems. The case affects organizations running vulnerable Marimo software and shows that experienced people can move extremely quickly without relying on AI tools, making fast fixes and protection of stored credentials important. The article also describes a separate campaign that used poorly protected Redis servers to install cryptocurrency-mining software on thousands of machines.

Summary
Sysdig observed a skilled human attacker exploit the critical Marimo RCE flaw CVE-2026-39987 and pivot to an SSH bastion via AWS Secrets Manager credentials in just eight seconds, using hand-written tooling rather than AI. The report underscores that rapid, evasive post-exploitation remains achievable without agentic attack frameworks.

Sysdig reported that a threat actor exploited CVE-2026-39987, a pre-authentication remote code execution flaw affecting all versions of Marimo, to gain an interactive shell on a compromised system. The attacker then used credentials harvested from that system to query AWS Secrets Manager, obtain an SSH private key, and authenticate to a bastion host. Sysdig observed the credential lookup four seconds after a fresh WebSocket connection and SSH authentication four seconds later, for an eight-second pivot.

The attacker operated for roughly nine hours, issued more than 850 interactive commands, and used hand-written scripts rather than recognizable public offensive tools or an AI agent. Sysdig said the operator avoided a trap that every agentic threat actor it had profiled against the same flaw fell into, highlighting that skilled human operators can move quickly and evade detections. Separately, Hunt.io reported a cryptomining campaign compromising 3,562 Redis servers, primarily using Redis rogue replication via the SLAVEOF command to deploy an XMRig miner; it attributed the affected systems to missing authentication rather than a version-specific Redis flaw.

  • Sysdig found that a human-operated, hand-built Python workflow reached the SSH bastion at a speed typically associated with AI-assisted activity, demonstrating that rapid intrusion response cannot focus only on agentic threats.
  • The operator avoided a trap that Sysdig said every agentic threat actor it profiled against the same Marimo flaw had entered, suggesting that manual operators may not follow the same detectable patterns as automated ones.
  • In the Redis campaign, rogue replication was the only technique that worked at scale, while SSH key injection, MongoDB sandbox-escape attempts, and the recovered WordPress chain did not produce confirmed large-scale results.
  • The Redis victims spanned versions from 2015 through 2023 and several Linux generations, with Hunt.io attributing the exposure primarily to missing authentication rather than a single software-version defect.
Key Points
  • 01Sysdig reported that a threat actor exploited CVE-2026-39987, a pre-authentication remote-code-execution flaw affecting all Marimo versions, to obtain an interactive shell on a compromised system.
  • 02Using credentials harvested from the compromised instance, the attacker called AWS Secrets Manager, retrieved an SSH private key, and authenticated to a bastion host within eight seconds of the initial WebSocket connection.
  • 03The attacker spent roughly nine hours in the environment, issued more than 850 interactive commands, and used hand-written Python scripts rather than recognizable public offensive tools or an AI agent.
  • 04Hunt.io identified a cryptomining campaign affecting 3,562 Redis servers, primarily using Redis rogue replication through the SLAVEOF command to deploy an XMRig miner.
  • 05Hunt.io said the affected Redis systems ranged from Redis 2.8.17 to 7.2.0, indicating that missing authentication rather than a version-specific flaw was the principal weakness.

In plain words

Hackers are actively targeting WordPress websites that use an older version of the paid WooCommerce Wholesale Lead Capture plugin. A flaw lets an outsider upload a hidden control program to the website, which can reveal information about the site and let the attacker add more harmful files. Website owners should update the plugin to version 2.0.3.2 or newer and check for unfamiliar files or administrator accounts, because an attacker could take full control of an affected site.

Summary
Attackers are actively exploiting CVE-2026-27540 in WooCommerce Wholesale Lead Capture versions 2.0.3.1 and earlier to upload PHP webshells and potentially fully compromise WordPress sites. Administrators should update to version 2.0.3.2 or later and investigate upload directories and AJAX logs for signs of compromise.

Attackers are actively exploiting CVE-2026-27540, a critical flaw in the WooCommerce Wholesale Lead Capture premium plugin for WordPress. The issue affects version 2.0.3.1 and older and can allow an unauthenticated attacker to upload PHP backdoors, potentially resulting in complete site compromise. Wordfence said its web application firewall blocked more than 100,000 attempts linked to the vulnerability, with activity spikes from June 4 to June 17 and on July 1 and August 30.

The flaw stems from an unauthenticated AJAX action, wwlc_file_upload_handler, that uses a file-type allowlist provided through the user-controlled file_settings parameter. Attackers can add PHP to that allowlist and upload a webshell that gathers host information and offers a browser-based form to upload further malicious files. Version 2.0.3.2, released February 20, fixes the issue; administrators are advised to update, inspect uploads and logs for suspicious activity, remove unknown administrator accounts, and restore from a safe backup if compromise is confirmed.

  • The upload restriction can be bypassed because the plugin trusts a file-type allowlist supplied by the person making the request, allowing attackers to add “php” as an accepted type.
  • The uploaded shell does more than collect information about the affected website: it also provides a browser-based form for placing additional malicious files on the site.
  • If a site is confirmed compromised, the article recommends restoring from a known-safe backup rather than relying only on deleting suspicious files, because hidden access mechanisms and unauthorized users may be difficult to fully remove.
  • Requests to WordPress’s admin-ajax.php endpoint that invoke wwlc_file_upload_handler are a specific log indicator administrators can use to investigate attempted or successful abuse.
Key Points
  • 01Attackers are actively exploiting CVE-2026-27540, an unauthenticated file-upload flaw in WooCommerce Wholesale Lead Capture plugin versions 2.0.3.1 and earlier.
  • 02The flaw lets attackers manipulate a user-controlled setting so the plugin accepts uploaded PHP files, enabling them to place webshells on vulnerable WordPress sites.
  • 03WooCommerce Wholesale Lead Capture version 2.0.3.2, released February 20, fixes the vulnerability.
  • 04Wordfence blocked more than 100,000 exploit attempts and reported spikes in activity from June 4 to June 17, as well as on July 1 and August 30.
  • 05Administrators are advised to update the plugin, check upload directories and logs for suspicious activity, remove unknown administrator accounts, and restore from a safe backup if compromise is confirmed.

Summary
Acronis says attackers have targeted a high-severity local privilege-escalation flaw (CVE-2026-87886) in its cPanel/WHM and Plesk backup plugins. Administrators should immediately update to Acronis Backup plugin for cPanel & WHM 1.9.3 HF3 or Plesk extension 1.8.11.

Acronis has disclosed CVE-2026-87886, a high-severity Linux local privilege-escalation flaw affecting its backup plugin for cPanel & WHM and its extension for Plesk. The company assigned the issue a CVSS score of 7.8 and says exploitation has been detected in limited, targeted attacks against Acronis Backup plugin for cPanel & WHM deployments. Acronis said this assessment is based on a single report from a potentially affected customer.

An attacker with limited permissions on a vulnerable Linux server could use the flaw to obtain greater access, potentially view or modify sensitive data, and disrupt the system without user interaction. Affected versions include cPanel & WHM plugin builds earlier than 1.9.3.1021, fixed in version 1.9.3 HF3, and Plesk extension builds earlier than 1.8.11.638, fixed in version 1.8.11. Acronis has not provided technical details or specific indicators of compromise and recommends affected users install the available updates immediately.

  • Acronis’ statement that exploitation was seen in the wild is based on a single report from a potentially affected customer, so the reported activity is limited in both scale and available confirmation.
  • Acronis has provided no specific indicators of compromise and has withheld technical details, making immediate installation of the available updates the main response described in the article.
  • The affected software is Acronis’ backup integration for cPanel & WHM and Plesk rather than the cPanel & WHM or Plesk platforms themselves.
  • The vulnerability can be used without user interaction after an attacker has limited access to a vulnerable Linux server, increasing the urgency for affected deployments.

In plain words

LiteSpeed warned that an older version of its paid web-server software has a serious weakness that could let someone with one website account take full control of a shared hosting machine. That could expose or let them change other customers’ websites and the server’s own files, even where the hosting provider uses tools meant to keep accounts separate. Hosting companies using LiteSpeed Enterprise should install version 6.3.7 promptly, since it may not arrive automatically right away.

Summary
LiteSpeed Web Server Enterprise versions before 6.3.7 contain a critical flaw that could allow a low-privilege shared-hosting account to gain root access and bypass isolation controls such as CageFS. Administrators should manually update to version 6.3.7 immediately because auto-update availability may be delayed.

A critical flaw in LiteSpeed Web Server Enterprise versions before 6.3.7 could allow a low-privilege hosting account to gain root access on a shared server, cPanel warned in a September 14 advisory. An attacker could then access or alter other customers’ sites and the server itself. The flaw can bypass account-isolation controls including CloudLinux CageFS, which normally restricts each hosting account’s view of the system.

LiteSpeed released version 6.3.7 on September 11, and both LiteSpeed and cPanel advised administrators to manually install it with /usr/local/lsws/admin/misc/lsup.sh -f -v 6.3.7. Automatic delivery may be delayed, and LiteSpeed’s download page still listed 6.3.6 as stable as of September 15. Neither company disclosed how the flaw works, assigned a CVE or severity score, stated whether it has been exploited, or provided indicators for determining whether systems were compromised.

  • Administrators who force the 6.3.7 update must later run touch /usr/local/lsws/autoupdate/follow_stable to resume following LiteSpeed’s stable automatic update tier.
  • As of September 15, LiteSpeed’s download page still listed 6.3.6 as stable, so relying on the usual stable-release listing could leave servers on an affected version.
  • The advisory does not clarify whether the 6.4.0 release candidates are affected, despite their changelog not listing the three security changes included in 6.3.7.
  • This is the third LiteSpeed-related root-access issue on cPanel servers reported since May, but it is the first described as affecting the LiteSpeed web server itself rather than the user-end cPanel plugin.

U.S., U.K., and Dutch agencies say Iran’s Ministry of Intelligence and Security has used Windows malware called HEAVYGRAM, or CHOSEN BRICK, to spy on dissidents, journalists, activists, and other people whose views conflict with the Iranian government. The campaign has targeted people in the United States, United Kingdom, Netherlands, and elsewhere, with the wider activity dated to autumn 2023 and CHOSEN BRICK use reported since at least 2025. It also creates Windows startup entries and excludes folders from Microsoft Defender scanning to remain active after a restart.

  • Each infected computer receives its own Telegram bot, a design the agencies say prevents one victim’s activity from being mixed with another’s.

In plain words

Attackers are automatically searching for Vite development servers that were accidentally made reachable from the internet. A flaw in Vite can let them read files that should be blocked, including settings files containing Amazon Web Services or Microsoft Azure account details, passwords, and other cloud secrets. This affects developers and organizations that expose these servers and keep sensitive files in accessible locations, and the stolen information could give criminals access to databases, cloud systems, and other company infrastructure.

Summary
Attackers are mass-scanning internet-exposed Vite development servers to exploit CVE-2026-39364, bypassing file-deny rules with query parameters to steal .env files, cloud credentials, and infrastructure configuration data. Organizations should keep Vite dev servers off public networks and apply the available fix.

F5 Labs reported an August 2026 mass-scanning campaign targeting Vite development servers that are exposed to the internet. The activity exploits CVE-2026-39364, a high-severity Vite flaw with a CVSS score of 8.2. Attackers are seeking cloud credentials, configuration data, and infrastructure state files from affected systems.

The flaw allows unauthenticated requests to retrieve files that should be blocked by Vite’s server.fs.deny setting when query parameters such as ?raw, ?import&raw, or ?import&url&inline are appended. A deployment is affected when its Vite development server is exposed to the network, the target file is within allowed directories, and the file matches a denied-file pattern. Observed requests targeted environment files, AWS and Azure profiles, Terraform state files, and system paths including /etc/passwd and /proc/self/environ.

The requests used fake User-Agent strings impersonating major web crawlers and AI bots, along with forged X-Forwarded-For and X-Real-IP values intended to bypass IP-based controls and complicate log analysis. Much of the observed malicious activity originated from the United States, Belgium, the Netherlands, Singapore, and Taiwan, with Google Cloud Platform address ranges used by the attackers. Exposing Vite through the --host flag, server.host settings, or incorrect Docker port mappings can make a development server reachable outside its default localhost configuration.

  • The flaw is most relevant when a Vite development server has been deliberately or accidentally exposed beyond localhost, including through Docker port-mapping mistakes, rather than under Vite's default local-only configuration.
  • By requesting /proc/self/cwd/.env, attackers can read the active environment file relative to the running application process without first knowing the application's full path.
  • The malicious requests impersonated well-known search and AI bots and included forged client-IP headers, which can make traffic appear less suspicious and complicate log review.
  • The campaign sought infrastructure state files such as terraform.tfstate and serverless.yml in addition to credentials, potentially exposing detailed cloud configuration information.
Key Points
  • 01F5 Labs observed an August 2026 mass-scanning campaign targeting internet-exposed Vite development servers to steal cloud credentials, configuration data, and infrastructure state files.
  • 02The campaign exploits CVE-2026-39364, a Vite flaw that can allow unauthenticated attackers to retrieve files blocked by server.fs.deny by adding query parameters such as ?raw or ?import&raw.
  • 03Affected deployments require the Vite development server to be exposed to the network, the sensitive file to be within server.fs.allow directories, and the file to match a server.fs.deny pattern.
  • 04Observed requests targeted environment files, AWS credentials and configurations, Terraform state files, Azure profiles, and system files such as /etc/passwd and /proc/self/environ.
  • 05The requests used spoofed crawler and AI-bot User-Agent strings and forged X-Forwarded-For and X-Real-IP values, while much of the activity originated from the United States, Belgium, the Netherlands, Singapore, and Taiwan.

In plain words

Someone broke into the website that distributes the paid Admin Menu Editor Pro add-on for WordPress and sent customers infected updates. The updates secretly gave the intruder a way to control affected websites and created hidden user accounts, affecting at least 230 customers and 1,500 sites, with potentially more impacted. Website owners who installed versions 2.35 or 2.36 should restore a safe backup or remove the infected files and accounts, because the intruder may still be able to access their sites.

Summary
Compromised updates for Admin Menu Editor Pro versions 2.35 and 2.36 installed a web shell and hidden WordPress users on potentially more than 1,500 sites. Customers should restore from a known-safe backup or remove the plugin, malicious object-cache directory, and related database entries.

An unauthorized party compromised the adminmenueditor.com website and distributed malicious updates for the paid Admin Menu Editor Pro WordPress plugin. Version 2.35 was available from about 06:00 to 13:00 UTC, and the developer’s clean 2.36 replacement was also compromised because the attacker still had access. The developer took the website offline after evidence suggested the attacker may have had root-level server access.

The malicious updates included includes/wp-user-consent.php, which installed a web shell and created a hidden user account on affected websites. Approximately 230 customers installed the first malicious version on at least 1,500 sites, while several hundred additional customers may have downloaded a trojanized version 2.36. Customers using versions 2.35 or 2.36 should restore from a safe backup made before September 14, or remove the plugin, /wp-content/object-cache/, and the identified malicious database entries; version 2.34 and the free plugin are believed to be unaffected.

  • Installing the initially clean version 2.36 was not necessarily safe because the attacker retained access to the update website and compromised that release as well.
  • The malicious user account may not appear in the WordPress dashboard, so checking only the visible user list could miss evidence of compromise.
  • The developer took the distribution website offline because the investigation suggested the attacker may have had root-level server access, indicating the issue could not be contained by simply removing one malicious update.
  • Version 2.34 is believed to be clean and the free Admin Menu Editor plugin does not appear to be affected, narrowing the incident to specific Pro releases.

In plain words

The article says that many online casino sites that look alike are used for very different crimes: moving illegal money, tricking gamblers out of deposits, or secretly supporting spying and break-ins at organizations. Some China-aligned groups hide their communications inside Chinese-language casino and adult sites, making them easy to overlook as mere gambling content. This affects casino customers who may lose money, as well as schools, banks, government agencies, IT companies, and other organizations whose networks may be contacted by the hidden spying infrastructure. The larger concern is that millions of rapidly changing websites, often using major hosting and domain-registration companies, make these criminal operations difficult to block one site at a time.

Summary
Infoblox found that millions of lookalike casino websites conceal distinct criminal operations, including illegal gambling and money laundering, scam gambling, and China-aligned PeckBirdy malware C2 infrastructure. Defenders should not dismiss casino or adult-domain activity as policy violations, because repeated queries to multiple PeckBirdy C2 domains may indicate a compromise.

Infoblox describes three kinds of malicious casino websites that can appear nearly identical in a browser: illegal Chinese-language casinos supporting gambling and money laundering, scam gambling sites that block withdrawals, and decoy sites used by China-aligned actors running the PeckBirdy command-and-control framework. The company tracks more than 1.7 million illegal Chinese-language casino domains, while the PeckBirdy population consists of dozens of decoy domains. These sites use rapidly changing domains, varied hosting providers, and customer-facing branding that can make criminal infrastructure hard to distinguish from ordinary low-quality gambling content.

PeckBirdy has operated since 2023 and embeds its communications infrastructure in Chinese-language casino and adult websites. Infoblox identified domains including cache-mcp[.]com and mcp-source[.]online; the latter had zero VirusTotal detections as of August 2026 despite being used for WebSocket connections. Just over 3% of Infoblox enterprise customers resolved at least one PeckBirdy command-and-control domain, with education, IT, banking, financial services, and government among the observed industries. Infoblox advises defenders not to dismiss casino or adult-domain alerts automatically, especially when a network contacts several distinct PeckBirdy domains.

  • The casino decoys used by PeckBirdy are visually indistinguishable from illegal gambling and scam sites, so dismissing a casino-domain alert as employee browsing can overlook malicious activity.
  • A single query to githubassets[.]net is weak evidence because the domain also receives accidental typo-related traffic, while queries to three to ten distinct PeckBirdy domains are a more meaningful compromise signal.
  • The four largest Chinese-language casino clusters account for roughly 99.5% of the domains Infoblox tracks, suggesting that a small number of operators underpin most of this very large ecosystem.
  • Domain blocking alone has limited effect against illegal casino networks because operators maintain thousands of domains and rapidly rotate to replacements when a site is blocked.
  • Many domains are registered through U.S. registrars while being hosted in China or Hong Kong, creating potential disruption opportunities through the registration providers even when the hosting is outside U.S. reach.

In plain words

Silent Push found thousands of fake websites used to steal banking information, with a major campaign impersonating Canadian banks, Canada Post, tax services, and benefit programs. The criminals keep these sites hard to shut down by constantly moving them among changing internet addresses and showing harmless “not found” pages to many visitors, while intended victims see convincing fake login or support pages. People in Canada, the United Kingdom, the United States, Australia, and Europe may be targeted, and some victims could be tricked into calling fake fraud hotlines or downloading harmful software. The findings matter because these operations can evade ordinary website blocks and scanners, allowing criminals to steal credentials and take over accounts at scale.

Summary
Silent Push identified thousands of phishing domains using commercial fast-flux infrastructure, including a large Canada-focused banking campaign that evades scanners through traffic cloaking and rapidly rotating IP addresses. The research highlights DNS delegation and IP/ASN diversity as key indicators defenders can use to detect and block this infrastructure proactively.

Silent Push investigated commercial fast-flux services by becoming a customer and studying how customer domains are routed through rapidly changing IP addresses and networks. Using DNS delegation signatures together with IP and ASN diversity scoring, it identified thousands of live phishing domains from a single platform query. One cluster targeted nearly 2,000 domains, with roughly nine in ten impersonating Canadian organizations including major banks, Canada Post, tax authorities, and provincial benefit programs.

The Canada-focused operation places domains behind Keitaro traffic-distribution cloaking, giving qualifying Canadian residential visitors single-use phishing URLs while many scanners, researchers, and foreign visitors receive a 404 page. A second cluster combines cloned login pages, fake fraud hotlines, live chat, one-time codes, and password-protected ZIP files containing a Windows executable. The article recommends DNS-level detection for high IP and ASN diversity, low TTLs, and inconsistent geolocation, as well as blocking domains and known abuse-tolerant infrastructure associated with the fast-flux services.

  • The fast-flux providers protect their own infrastructure by keeping their domains separate from customer sites, but the required customer delegation to provider-controlled DNS creates a detectable signature.
  • The Canada-focused phishing operation uses per-victim, single-use web addresses that are burned after issuance, helping it limit exposure to security scanners and researchers.
  • The callback phishing cluster combines credential theft with live phone or chat engagement, and only provides a malicious download after a live agent issues a valid one-time code.
  • The phishing infrastructure mixes abuse-tolerant networks with ordinary hosting providers, so blocking only known bulletproof networks would not cover every address used in the rotating pool.
  • The article states that domains can be identified as soon as they are delegated to the fast-flux nameservers, before the first phishing lure is sent.

In plain words

Researchers found that Parallels Desktop 26.4.0 on Mac computers can let an ordinary local user run their own program with full control of the computer. The issue affects Macs with the Parallels background service enabled, even when no virtual machine is running, and does not require the user to be a Parallels customer or administrator. This matters because harmful software arriving through a compromised developer tool, download, or shared account could take over the whole Mac, access other users’ data, and remain installed. Parallels released a fix in version 27.0.0.

Summary
Parallels Desktop 26.4.0 for macOS contains CVE-2026-90894, a local privilege-escalation flaw that lets an unprivileged user abuse the world-writable root-service socket and tar argument injection to execute code as root. Organizations should upgrade to Parallels Desktop 27.0.0 or later and restrict local access to affected Macs.

JFrog researchers reported CVE-2026-90894, a local privilege-escalation issue in Parallels Desktop 26.4.0 build 57513 on Apple silicon. An unprivileged local user could execute code as root through Parallels’ privileged prl_disp_service helper. The reported attack does not require administrator rights, a Parallels-signed client, or a running virtual machine.

The exploit chain connects to the world-writable /var/run/prl_disp_service.socket and uses PrlSrv_LoginLocal, which the researchers said accepted an unsigned local client based on peer credentials. A specially crafted appliance-install parent path injects tar’s --use-compress-program option during archive extraction, causing a root-launched tar process to run an attacker-controlled script. The article says this could allow harmful code already running as a local user to take over the Mac, read other users’ data, and establish persistence; Parallels released a fix in Parallels Desktop 27.0.0.

  • A running virtual machine is not required for the reported privilege escalation because the root dispatcher service normally starts when Parallels Desktop is loaded.
  • The local client does not need to be signed by Parallels or have administrator rights: the article reports that LoginLocal accepted an unsigned, non-admin client based on its local system credentials.
  • The appliance-install operation may return an extraction error after the attacker-controlled script has already run as root, so an apparent installation failure does not necessarily mean the attempted abuse was unsuccessful.
  • A practical exposure check is whether /var/run/prl_disp_service.socket is world-writable with mode 0777, particularly on or near the lab-tested Parallels Desktop 26.4.0 build 57513.
  • The injected tar option runs a separate program outside the archive itself, meaning the harmful script does not need to be packaged inside the appliance file.
Key Points
  • 01JFrog researchers reported that Parallels Desktop 26.4.0 build 57513 on Apple silicon allowed an unprivileged local user to execute code as root through the prl_disp_service helper.
  • 02The reported chain uses the world-writable /var/run/prl_disp_service.socket, an unsigned PrlSrv_LoginLocal session that succeeds using peer credentials, and argument injection in the InstallAppliance extraction path.
  • 03A quote in the appliance parent-path value can inject tar’s --use-compress-program option, causing macOS tar launched by the root service to run an attacker-controlled script as root.
  • 04The article identifies the issue as CVE-2026-90894 and says Parallels released a fix in Parallels Desktop 27.0.0 on September 1, 2026.
  • 05The article recommends inventorying Macs with Parallels Desktop, restricting local-account access, and upgrading to a fixed version.
OPEN SOURCE ↗
JUSTIFICATION

This is a detailed report of a concrete local privilege-escalation vulnerability in Parallels Desktop that allows a non-admin local user to obtain root access. It is broadly relevant to organizations with Parallels-installed Macs and includes a fixed version and practical exposure indicators, though the article does not report active exploitation in the wild.

Summary
Oracle's September 2026 Critical Security Patch Update delivers 673 patches for 672 CVEs across 17 product families, including 104 critical-severity fixes. Oracle E-Business Suite and Fusion Middleware account for the largest shares of the updates.

Oracle released its September 2026 Critical Security Patch Update on September 15, providing 673 security updates for 672 unique CVEs across 17 Oracle product families. The release includes 104 critical-severity patches, 503 high-severity patches, 59 medium-severity patches, and seven low-severity patches. Oracle introduced monthly CSPUs in May 2026 as a faster release cycle between its larger quarterly Critical Patch Updates.

Oracle E-Business Suite received the largest number of updates, with 159 patches, followed by Oracle Fusion Middleware with 153. Fusion Middleware also has the highest listed number of issues that can be exploited over a network without authentication, at 78, while Oracle Hyperion has 50 such issues and E-Business Suite has 19. Oracle has made patches and additional details available through its September 2026 advisory and risk matrices.

  • Oracle E-Business Suite and Oracle Fusion Middleware together account for 312 of the 673 updates, nearly half of the entire September 2026 release.
  • Oracle Fusion Middleware has the highest listed count of issues reachable remotely without signing in, at 78, despite E-Business Suite receiving the most total patches.
  • Oracle Hyperion has 50 issues listed as remotely reachable without authentication from 102 total patches, making this exposure notable relative to its patch volume.
  • Although critical fixes receive emphasis, high-severity issues make up the largest portion of the release, with 503 of 673 patches.

In plain words

Researchers uncovered KREMLIN, a banking-focused criminal program that tricks people with fake bank, invoice, or company files and then adds a harmful extension to Chrome or Edge. The extension can steal passwords, login-session information, browsing data, screenshots, and the contents of web pages, with more than 98% of identified infected computers located in Brazil. This matters because stolen login sessions can let criminals access accounts even without a password, while the group’s use of blockchain-based online instructions makes its control servers harder to shut down.

Summary
Elastic researchers uncovered KREMLIN, a Brazilian banking-malware operation that installs malicious Chrome and Edge extensions to steal credentials, cookies, session tokens, and browser data. The campaign uses multi-stage loaders, DLL sideloading, Chromium preference-integrity bypasses, and Ethereum smart contracts to dynamically hide its command-and-control infrastructure.

Elastic Security Labs has identified REF9334, a Brazilian banking-malware operation active since at least May 2025 that delivers a toolkit called KREMLIN. The campaign uses files disguised as banking, invoice, or company documents to begin a multi-stage infection process. It impersonates a dozen Brazilian banks and installs a malicious extension in Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge to steal credentials, session tokens, and other sensitive browser data.

KREMLIN uses JavaScript loaders, a custom C++ installer, DLL sideloading through a legitimate SentinelOne binary, and checks intended to avoid sandboxes and virtual machines. It retrieves command-and-control and payload-hosting locations from Ethereum smart contracts, allowing operators to update infrastructure dynamically. The installed extension, named AVSync System Inc., can collect cookies, session and local storage, screenshots, tab information, page HTML, and intercepted requests; Elastic observed 1,515 systems contacting its network canary domain, with more than 98% geolocated in Brazil.

  • Elastic registered the malware’s unregistered-domain network canary, causing infected systems that receive a valid response to deliberately crash and potentially giving defenders more time to find and remediate them.
  • KREMLIN checks whether its malicious browser extension is already installed and downloads it only when it is absent or its version differs from the version supplied by the attacker-controlled server.
  • Although the extension attempts to collect up to 1,000 browser-history entries from the prior 15 days, the researchers noted that this likely fails because its manifest does not request the required history permission.
  • The campaign’s use of Ethereum smart contracts to retrieve hosting and command-and-control locations began on May 19, 2026, after earlier activity involving malicious extensions and off-the-shelf remote-access Trojans.
Key Points
  • 01Elastic Security Labs identified REF9334, an operation active since at least May 2025 that uses KREMLIN banking malware against targets impersonating Brazilian banks.
  • 02KREMLIN begins with a JavaScript file disguised as a banking, invoice, or company document and uses multi-stage loaders, custom C++ installers, and anti-sandbox checks to install additional payloads.
  • 03The malware uses Ethereum smart contracts to obtain updated command-and-control and payload-hosting locations, making its infrastructure more difficult to disrupt.
  • 04KREMLIN installs a malicious Chrome and Edge extension named AVSync System Inc. by modifying Chromium Secure Preferences and forging the metadata required to bypass browser integrity protections.
  • 05The malicious extension can steal cookies, session storage, local storage, page HTML, screenshots, tab information, and other browser data; Elastic observed 1,515 systems checking a network canary domain, with more than 98% geolocated in Brazil.
OPEN SOURCE ↗
JUSTIFICATION

This is an active, named banking-malware operation using malicious Chrome and Edge extensions to steal credentials and session tokens, primarily affecting systems in Brazil. Its use of Chromium integrity bypasses, DLL sideloading, and Ethereum smart contracts for resilient command-and-control makes the findings broadly useful for defenders, though the observed targeting is geographically concentrated.

    In plain words

    Researchers found BambooToken, a previously unknown program that can secretly take instructions from its operators and collect information from Windows and Linux computers. It has been used since at least 2023 against organizations in Asia and South America, including mobile-app services, hotels, finance groups, and other businesses. The operators appear to hide the program inside software used with Tendyron OnKey security USB devices and communicate through a common lightweight messaging method, making the activity harder to spot. The stolen information could reveal people’s movements and travel plans, financial transactions, and patterns of daily life.

    Summary
    Researchers uncovered BambooToken, a Windows and Linux malware family active since 2023 that uses MQTT for command-and-control and DLL sideloading of Tendyron OnKey components to evade detection. The campaign has targeted organizations across Asia and South America, apparently for broad data collection.

    Researchers at Lumen Black Lotus Labs disclosed BambooToken, a previously undocumented malware family that has targeted Windows and Linux systems since at least February 2023. The campaign uses the lightweight MQTT messaging protocol to receive instructions from its operators and has affected organizations across Asia and South America. Its initial delivery method is unknown, and activity was detected as recently as July 2026.

    Early BambooToken versions used a PowerShell-based launcher, while later versions used DLL sideloading involving Tendyron OnKeySrv and a rogue OnKeyToken_KEB.dll file. The malware collects host information, can manage plug-ins, and includes a Windows plug-in that identifies installed antivirus products through WMI before sending the results to its command server. Identified affected entities include mobile-application-related servers, a hotel, finance organizations, a GitLab server, and companies in several countries; Lumen said the targeting could support collection of information about mobile use, financial transactions, and travel.

    • BambooToken evolved from a PowerShell-based launcher to DLL sideloading of a legitimate Tendyron OnKey component, a change Lumen assessed as likely to produce fewer endpoint-detection alerts.
    • The campaign expanded to Linux hosts by December 2025 while retaining MQTT for control, making it a cross-platform operation rather than a Windows-only threat.
    • One campaign domain rose into Cloudflare Radar’s top 500,000 domains, while an older domain reached the top 1 million during 2024, which Lumen said indicates widespread infections across the activity cluster.
    • The malware includes a Windows plugin specifically designed to inventory installed antivirus products through WMI and send the results to its command server.
    • Most BambooToken samples were uploaded to VirusTotal from Chinese IP address space, which the researchers said indicates a data-collection campaign focused on users in China and neighboring countries.
    Key Points
    • 01Lumen Black Lotus Labs identified BambooToken, a previously undocumented malware family that has been active since at least February 2023 and targets Windows and Linux systems using MQTT for command-and-control communications.
    • 02The campaign has targeted organizations in Asia and South America, with identified affected entities including mobile-application-related servers, a Hong Kong GitLab server, a Vietnamese hotel, an Argentine biomedical company, a Chilean legal firm, a Lithuanian cryptocurrency website, and a Malaysian financial organization.
    • 03BambooToken later versions use DLL sideloading through Tendyron OnKeySrv and a rogue OnKeyToken_KEB.dll file, while the earlier version was launched by a PowerShell-based stager.
    • 04The malware collects host details and can deploy a Windows plugin that uses WMI to identify installed antivirus products and send that information to its command server.
    • 05Lumen said the campaign’s combination of MQTT-based control and Cloudflare-routed infrastructure enables large-scale operations and may support collection of data related to mobile use, financial transactions, and travel.

    This is a newly disclosed, active cross-platform malware campaign using MQTT command-and-control and DLL sideloading, with identified targets across Asia and South America. In plain words

Researchers found a previously unknown program called BambooToken that lets attackers remotely control infected Windows and Linux computers by sending messages through a service commonly used for connected devices. It has been linked to about a dozen affected organizations, mainly in Asia and South America, including hotels, medical companies, law firms, financial organizations, mobile-app backend systems, and a GitLab server in Hong Kong. The attackers may be able to collect system details, run commands, and move or delete files, while code also suggests possible spying features such as recording keystrokes, audio, webcam video, and screenshots. This matters because the messaging-based setup can make the attackers harder to track and lets their access keep working through temporary network interruptions.

Summary
BambooToken is a cross-platform malware framework that uses MQTT for resilient command-and-control of Windows and Linux systems, with infections linked to DLL side-loading through Tendyron OnKey software and Kingsoft Office impersonation. Lumen identified roughly a dozen compromised organizations, largely in Asia and South America, and says the targeting may be consistent with China-aligned activity.

BambooToken is a previously unknown malware framework active since at least 2023 that communicates with Windows and Linux systems using MQTT, a lightweight messaging protocol commonly designed for connected devices. Variants developed between 2024 and 2025 use MQTT for command-and-control communications, with infected machines subscribing to topics tied to a unique identifier. Operators publish commands to those topics, while the malware sends status and system information through the central message broker.

Lumen’s Black Lotus Labs reported that infections occurred through side-loading with digitally signed Tendyron OnKey USB-token software or by impersonating Kingsoft Office. A Linux BambooToken 2.1 sample observed in December 2025 can collect extensive system information, open a command shell, and upload, download, or delete files, although researchers said it appeared to be under development. Lumen identified roughly a dozen compromised enterprise entities, mostly in Asia and South America, including mobile-app backend servers and a GitLab server in Hong Kong; it could not attribute the activity to a specific actor, but said the targeting patterns were consistent with China-aligned operations.

  • By using MQTT topics through a central broker instead of directly contacting attacker infrastructure, BambooToken can make its communications more evasive and remain operational through temporary network disruptions.
  • Strings suggesting surveillance features such as keylogging, webcam capture, and audio recording were found only in dead code, so researchers could not confirm that these capabilities existed in deployed attacks.
  • The most frequently compromised servers were associated with mobile application backend infrastructure, indicating that this environment was a prominent target in the observed activity.
  • The compromise of a GitLab server in Hong Kong created a potential foothold for supply-chain attacks, according to Lumen.
  • The newest Linux BambooToken sample, seen in December 2025, supports command shells and file upload, download, and deletion, but researchers assessed it as still under development.
Key Points
  • 01BambooToken is a previously unknown malware framework active since at least 2023 that uses the MQTT messaging protocol for command-and-control communications with Windows and Linux systems.
  • 02BambooToken variants developed between 2024 and 2025 subscribe infected machines to identifier-specific MQTT topics, allowing operators to publish commands and receive system status and information through a central broker.
  • 03Black Lotus Labs reported that BambooToken infections involved side-loading through digitally signed Tendyron OnKey USB-token software or impersonation of the Kingsoft Office productivity suite.
  • 04Researchers found a BambooToken plugin that enumerates antivirus products and dead-code strings referencing keylogging, clipboard theft, audio recording, webcam capture, and screenshot capture, but could not confirm those modules were used in attacks.
  • 05Lumen identified approximately a dozen compromised enterprise entities, mainly in Asia and South America, including a GitLab server in Hong Kong, and could not attribute the activity to a specific threat actor.
OPEN SOURCE ↗
JUSTIFICATION

This is a concrete report on an active, previously unknown cross-platform malware framework affecting enterprise entities and using an uncommon MQTT-based control channel. Security professionals should read it for the documented infection methods, Linux capabilities, affected environments, and available indicators of compromise.

Summary
A phishing email impersonating Squarespace used a real but dormant company domain to make a fake renewal demand seem credible, despite public records showing the domain was already renewed, registrar-locked against renewal, and held by another registrar. The case shows that checking a domain’s expiry, registrar, and registry status can quickly disprove renewal lures without clicking links.

In late August 2026, a shared partnerships mailbox at a global digital advertising agency received an urgent Squarespace-branded notice seeking $12.47 to renew a legacy domain by the next day. The domain was real and still owned by the organization, but it was no longer used for mail. Public registration data showed that it had been renewed months earlier, was paid into the following year, and was held by a registrar unrelated to Squarespace. Its registry status also included a renew-prohibited lock, meaning the requested renewal could not have been completed until that lock was removed.

The email used sender-controlled branding, including a Squarespace display name, organization header, copied postal addresses, and dead support and navigation links. It passed SPF, DKIM, and DMARC because those checks aligned with the attacker-controlled sending domain, not the impersonated Squarespace brand; replies were directed to an unrelated retailer mailbox. Its Renew Domain button led through a Google shortlink to a malicious Squarespace-branded domain, although the destination blocked the scanner from viewing its content. The article’s central lesson is that recipients can check a domain’s expiry date, registrar of record, and registry status codes through public records to disprove renewal, expiry, or suspension lures without clicking a link.

  • A highly personalized domain-renewal claim can be checked against public records, so the attacker’s use of a real dormant domain also created an easy way to disprove the lure.
  • A renew-prohibited registry lock made the requested payment action impossible for anyone to complete until the lock was deliberately removed, which is stronger evidence of fraud than an incorrect expiry date alone.
  • SPF, DKIM, and DMARC all passed because they validated the attacker-controlled sending domain, demonstrating that email authentication does not verify the brand displayed in the message.
  • The shortlink was classified as clean while its resolved destination was classified as malicious, showing that a reputation result for a redirect service does not establish that the final destination is safe.
  • The platform’s structural impersonation flag was false because the Squarespace identity was placed in sender-controlled display fields and copied address text rather than an identifiable lookalike sender domain.

  • 04The email authenticated with SPF, DKIM, and DMARC for the attacker-controlled sending domain, but those checks did not authenticate the Squarespace brand used in the message.

Summary
Censys identified 131 internet-exposed Mythic C2 hosts, most recognizable through default TLS certificates and port 7443 behavior. While some deployments appear to be labs, others show sophisticated operational infrastructure, making these fingerprints useful for proactive network and host-based detection.

Mythic is an open-source, plugin-based command-and-control framework used for authorized red-team work and also observed in unauthorized intrusions. As of September 11, 2026, Censys tracked 131 unique internet-exposed Mythic hosts across 307 service hits. Most of these hosts could be identified through default deployment fingerprints, including self-signed certificates with O=Mythic or O=Mythic C2, which appeared on 115 hosts.

Port 7443 appeared on 99 tracked hosts, and Mythic’s default Nginx reverse proxy returns HTTP 502 responses to unauthenticated requests on that port. Ten hosts also exposed other command-and-control frameworks, including Sliver, Adaptix C2, Havoc, and FRP; the article distinguishes an apparent multi-tool lab cluster from a separate cluster that used custom domains, custom payload development, Discord-related scripts, and Mythic tasking scripts. Censys recommends using certificate names, the default CN=operators to CN=multiplayer certificate chain, port 7443 activity, and unexpected Mythic Docker container names to detect potential Mythic infrastructure or internal systems communicating with it.

  • Default Mythic certificate subject organizations, "Mythic" and "Mythic C2," covered 115 of 131 tracked hosts, giving defenders a high-coverage way to identify many exposed deployments.
  • A shared nine-port fingerprint, identical self-signed certificate, generic reverse DNS, and multiple C2 frameworks across three hosts led the article to assess that cluster as a shared lab or training fleet rather than an operational deployment.
  • The article shows that a Mythic-only footprint can still support substantial custom tooling: one four-host cluster included eleven sequential Windows payload builds, Rust source code, Discord transport diagnostics, steganography scripts, and Mythic tasking scripts.
  • Only 6 tracked hosts retained Mythic’s unchanged internal certificate chain from "CN=operators" to "CN=multiplayer," making that combination a narrower but especially specific default-installation indicator.
  • Port-based counts should be interpreted carefully because the article’s port aggregation includes every open port on matched hosts, rather than proving that each port is a Mythic listener.

Cloudflare has introduced resource-level access controls for Workers, enabling customers to grant a teammate or API token access to one specific Worker rather than to all resources in an account. The release provides four roles: Metadata Read-Only, Content Read-Only, Editor, and Admin. Metadata Read-Only allows access to settings, metrics, logs, traces, and analytics without exposing source code, while Content Read-Only permits code review without changes or deployments. Summary
Trail of Bits argues that 1Password’s 26% AI clean-patch headline is misleading because it mixes deliberately wrong prompts and no-testing trials with normal repair attempts. Its reanalysis found 86% of appropriately configured agent patches blocked the supplied exploit, while emphasizing that both AI and human fixes still need rigorous validation and review.

Trail of Bits argues that 1Password’s report claiming AI models produced clean vulnerability fixes only 26% of the time is misleading. It says the benchmark selected six difficult fixes, included prompts telling agents to apply incorrect fixes, and combined trials where agents could test code with trials where they could not. In Trail of Bits’ reanalysis of trials where agents could run code and were not told to apply a wrong fix, 2,634 of 3,067 patches, or 86%, blocked the supplied exploit, although blocking an exploit does not prove a complete repair.

The article also says patch quality must be compared with human work under similar conditions: Trail of Bits found that 12.5% of first developer fixes in 2,265 vulnerabilities reviewed during client assessments did not fully resolve the issue. Its review of 186 closed or merged Patch the Planet pull requests found that maintainers merged 126, while later investigation identified functional, automation, and performance problems but no exploitable security vulnerabilities in the examined patches.   • The study’s automated reviewers matched human reviewers on the complete five-category outcome in only 65.9% of reviewed cases, and the two reviewing models assigned different outcomes to 36.8% of the same patches.

  • A Trail of Bits agent patch and an independent freenginx maintainer patch both introduced the same cleanup-time crash after addressing the original callback-lifetime bug.
  • Trail of Bits’ review of roughly 33,500 later commits affecting Patch the Planet projects found functional, build/test/release, and performance bugs in its patches, but found no exploitable security vulnerabilities.
  • The released post-patch-validation workflow requires a test to fail on the vulnerable version and pass on the patched version, plus a separate test of another path to the same underlying failure.

Attack Chains, Not Just Attack Surfaces: Why Testing Individual Techniques Misses the Point
thehackernews.com · 15 Sep 2026 11:26 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.6-terra
TAGScredential-harvestingdata-exfiltrationdirection-generale-des-finances-publiquesfiligranfrancelateral-movementmitre-att-ckopenaevspearphishingxtm-one
35
In plain words

The article argues that companies should not only check whether they can stop one harmful action at a time, because real intruders often combine many steps, such as tricking someone with an email, stealing a password, moving through company computers, and taking data. It says organizations can still suffer serious incidents even when individual defenses appear to work, citing a 2025 breach of France’s tax authority as an example. Filigran is promoting software that repeatedly imitates these full sequences so security teams can find the weak point that would let the whole chain succeed. The broader risk is that attackers, increasingly helped by AI, may move from an initial mistake to major damage faster than disconnected security checks can reveal the problem.

Summary
Testing isolated security techniques can miss the real risk: attackers chain multiple steps from phishing and credential theft through lateral movement and exfiltration. Filigran promotes OpenAEV Attack Chaining and XTM One as tools for continuously simulating these adaptive, end-to-end attack paths within defined safety controls.

The article argues that security testing focused on isolated techniques does not adequately measure whether an attacker can complete a multi-stage intrusion. It describes a typical sequence beginning with phishing and credential theft, followed by initial access, privilege escalation, lateral movement, data staging, and exfiltration. According to the article, individual controls may appear to work while gaps between tools, teams, and alerts still allow the overall sequence to succeed.

Filigran presents Attack Chaining in its OpenAEV platform as a way to automate conditional, end-to-end attack simulations. The system uses findings from one action, such as a valid credential, open port, token, or permission issue, to determine subsequent actions and displays the path in a live interactive graph. The article also describes operator-led and XTM One-powered autonomous modes, both bounded by defined targets, allowed actions, and escalation limits, with the goal of identifying chokepoints where a fix can stop the rest of an attack path.

  • A security program can report that individual controls passed their tests while still leaving an exploitable route across several weaknesses, because the decisive failure may occur in how the steps connect rather than in any single step.
  • The article identifies chokepoints as especially actionable remediation targets: fixing one point in an attack path can collapse every downstream step instead of requiring teams to address a long list of separate findings.
  • Treating a phishing click, reply, or submitted password as an input to the next simulated step allows social engineering to be evaluated as part of the same path as internal movement and data theft.
  • According to Filigran’s cited survey, 84% of security leaders identify siloed tools and disconnected testing as a major reason exposures remain unnoticed until they are exploited.
  • The article says autonomous chaining can be constrained by predefined targets, permitted actions, and escalation limits, allowing simulations to adapt while remaining within set boundaries.
Key Points
  • 01The article argues that testing individual security techniques in isolation does not show whether a multi-stage intrusion can succeed through gaps between controls, tools, teams, and alerts.
  • 02It describes attack chains as sequences that can begin with phishing and credential theft, then progress through initial access, privilege escalation, lateral movement, data staging, and data exfiltration.
  • 03Filigran’s OpenAEV Attack Chaining feature is presented as linking actions into conditional, end-to-end simulations that use the real results of one step to determine the next step.
  • 04The article says OpenAEV provides live attack-path graphs, structured findings to identify chokepoints, predefined scope and safety controls, and social-engineering stages such as phishing emails, SMS lures, and fake landing pages.
  • 05OpenAEV can run chains in an operator-led mode or in an autonomous mode using an XTM One-powered AI agent that plans, executes, and adapts the sequence within defined scope controls.

JUSTIFICATION

This is a vendor-promotional, evergreen perspective on testing multi-stage attack paths, not reporting a new incident, active threat, vulnerability, or patch. It may be useful to teams evaluating breach-and-attack simulation practices, but it has low urgency.
